triage.name: Acute Bronchitis
triage.reason: Very common cough illness where the key skill is distinguishing it from pneumonia and avoiding unnecessary antibiotics; reachable by history and exam.

demographics: Common in adults of all ages; one of the most frequent reasons for outpatient visits for cough
More frequent in winter and early spring, following the seasonal pattern of viral respiratory infections
Children are affected too, but the diagnosis is made less often because other causes of cough are more common in that age group

risk_factors.text: Recent viral upper respiratory infection or close contact with someone who has one
Cigarette smoking or exposure to secondhand smoke
Exposure to air pollution, dust, fumes or vapors
Crowded settings such as daycare, school, military barracks or dormitories

social_history: Secondhand smoke exposure at home or work
Occupational exposure to dust, fumes or vapors
exposures: Sick contacts with cough or cold symptoms

chief_complaints.text: I've had a cough that won't go away
My chest feels sore and tight when I cough
I've been wheezing and short of breath
I feel like I have a bad cold that moved into my chest

hpi.onset: Gradual, starting a few days after a cold or sore throat
hpi.duration: Cough present for about 1–3 weeks at presentation; often lasts 3–8 weeks total
hpi.progression: Begins as a dry, hacking cough, then becomes productive of clear, white or colored sputum; the cough is most bothersome in the first week and slowly improves, though it may linger for several weeks after other symptoms resolve
hpi.quality: Scratchy and dry at first, then loose and productive; may be paroxysmal
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; cough is annoying and disrupts sleep but does not limit daily activity
hpi.timing: Present throughout the day, often worse at night and on waking

associated_symptoms.text: Burning or soreness in the chest with coughing

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain that is sharp and worse with deep breath or lying flat
Recurrent episodes of wheeze and cough since childhood

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children cannot describe sputum or chest tightness; they present with a lingering cough after a cold, sometimes with vomiting after coughing spells. Wheezing is more prominent, and the cough may be mistaken for asthma or a foreign body.
Fever may be blunted or absent, and the cough can be less forceful. Symptoms overlap more with pneumonia, heart failure and COPD, so the threshold for chest imaging is lower.
The same symptoms can progress to pneumonia or be caused by unusual organisms; fever and systemic symptoms may be more prominent and the course more prolonged.
Presentation is similar, but cough and shortness of breath are more alarming because of the risk to the fetus; treatment choices are limited and pertussis should be considered.

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, speaking in full sentences; coughs intermittently during the visit
general.moderate: Mildly ill-appearing, coughs frequently and has to pause mid-sentence; no respiratory distress at rest
general.severe: Ill-appearing, flushed, tachypneic with visible effort on coughing; still able to speak in phrases
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, in respiratory distress; not expected in uncomplicated acute bronchitis and should prompt reassessment for pneumonia or another cause

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient during the interview and ask them to take a deep breath
findings.finding: Frequent cough, often productive of clear, white or colored sputum

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx with a light and tongue blade
findings.finding: Redness of the posterior pharynx without exudate
Swollen, congested nasal mucosa with clear or mucoid discharge

findings.maneuver: Inspect the tonsils and posterior pharynx
Palpate the anterior and posterior cervical chains
Inspect the neck with the patient at 45 degrees for jugular venous distension
Observe the patient's breathing at rest for use of the sternocleidomastoid and intercostal muscles
findings.finding: No use of accessory muscles of respiration

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields during quiet and deep breathing
Auscultate the lung fields and ask the patient to cough
findings.finding: Rhonchi that clear or shift with coughing

findings.maneuver: Palpate the chest while the patient speaks
Palpate the anterior chest wall and costochondral junctions
Palpate the right upper quadrant and percuss the liver span
findings.finding: No hepatomegaly or right upper quadrant tenderness

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of each foot and the pretibial area

labs.caveat: Low values support a viral cause and argue against bacterial pneumonia; a value above 0.25–0.5 ng/mL should prompt reconsideration of pneumonia. Not required for diagnosis.
Mildly elevated or normal; marked elevation suggests pneumonia rather than simple acute bronchitis.
Usually normal; mild leukocytosis can occur with viral illness and does not by itself indicate bacterial infection.
Relative lymphocytosis favors a viral cause.

imaging.preferred_when: When pneumonia is suspected (abnormal vital signs, focal lung findings, hypoxemia, or an older or immunocompromised patient)

findings.text: Normal lungs without consolidation, infiltrate or pleural effusion
Hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms in a patient with underlying COPD
Peribronchial thickening or increased bronchovascular markings (nonspecific)

imaging.preferred_when: Not routine; only when the chest x-ray is nondiagnostic or another process such as a mass, bronchiectasis or interstitial disease is suspected

initial.why: Distinguishes acute bronchitis from pneumonia; the main reason to image in a cough illness
initial.only_if: pneumonia is suspected (fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal crackles or dullness, or an older or immunocompromised patient)

supporting.why: Low value supports a viral cause and can help avoid antibiotics
supporting.only_if: the diagnosis is uncertain or antibiotic use is being considered

supporting.why: Identifies influenza when antiviral treatment would change management
supporting.only_if: influenza is circulating and the patient presents within the treatment window

supporting.test: Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viruses (multiplex PCR)
supporting.why: Identifies a specific viral cause when the result would change management
supporting.only_if: severe illness, immunocompromised patient, or an outbreak setting

supporting.why: Confirms whooping cough when paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting or a prolonged cough suggests it
Looks for a bacterial cause when bacterial infection is a real consideration
supporting.only_if: purulent sputum with a toxic appearance or a suspected bacterial pathogen

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management in an uncomplicated cough illness
Not needed unless the patient is dehydrated or severely ill
Not required for diagnosis; does not reliably separate viral bronchitis from pneumonia
Not routine; reserve for uncertain cases or antibiotic decisions
Not needed when the presentation is typical and pneumonia is not suspected
Not indicated for uncomplicated acute bronchitis
Not routine; most cases are viral
Not routine outside influenza season or when antivirals would not be used
No role unless pulmonary embolism is being considered
No role unless heart failure is being considered

decision_points: The diagnosis is clinical; imaging is only needed when pneumonia or another process is suspected
A normal chest x-ray in a patient with a compatible history supports acute bronchitis
Antibiotics are not indicated for viral acute bronchitis; reserve them for a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial cause such as pertussis
Consider pertussis when the cough is paroxysmal, lasts more than 2 weeks, or is accompanied by post-tussive vomiting

differential.name: Community-acquired pneumonia
differential.why_considered: The single most important look-alike: cough, fever, sputum and chest discomfort overlap completely with acute bronchitis.
differential.trigger: Fever above 100.4°F, tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal crackles, dullness to percussion or egophony

history: Higher fever with shaking chills
Shortness of breath at rest or with minimal activity
Pleuritic chest pain worse with deep breath
Feeling systemically very unwell rather than just a bad cold
exam: Tachypnea and use of accessory muscles
labs: Hypoxemia on pulse oximetry or arterial blood gas
imaging: Lobar or segmental consolidation on chest x-ray

differential.name: Influenza
differential.why_considered: A leading viral cause of acute bronchitis; presents with cough plus systemic symptoms, especially in winter.

history: Abrupt onset over hours rather than days
High fever, severe myalgias, headache and prostration
Cough may be dry and non-productive early
Known community outbreak or sick contacts
exam: Lung exam often clear or with minimal findings
labs: Positive rapid influenza antigen or molecular test
imaging: Chest x-ray normal unless complicated by pneumonia

differential.name: Asthma exacerbation
differential.why_considered: Cough, wheeze and chest tightness are shared, and viral infections commonly trigger asthma attacks.

history: Recurrent episodes of wheeze and cough since childhood
Known asthma diagnosis or prior inhaler use
Symptoms triggered by allergens, exercise or cold air
Nocturnal cough and wheeze
exam: Signs of atopy such as allergic rhinitis

differential.name: COPD exacerbation
differential.why_considered: Chronic productive cough with acute worsening, common in smokers and older adults.

history: Long-standing daily cough and sputum for years
Progressive exertional dyspnea
Heavy smoking history
Prior COPD diagnosis or inhaler use
exam: Diffuse wheeze and distant breath sounds
Use of accessory muscles at baseline
labs: Elevated CO2 on blood gas in advanced disease

differential.name: Pertussis (whooping cough)
differential.why_considered: Prolonged cough illness that can be mistaken for viral bronchitis, especially when the cough lingers for weeks.
differential.trigger: Paroxysmal cough lasting more than 2 weeks, post-tussive vomiting or inspiratory whoop

history: Cough comes in violent paroxysms
Post-tussive vomiting or whoop
Cough lasting more than 2 weeks
Close contact with a person who has a prolonged cough
Incomplete or unknown vaccination
exam: Conjunctival hemorrhage or facial petechiae from coughing
Lung exam often normal between spells
labs: Lymphocytosis with markedly elevated lymphocyte count
Positive pertussis PCR or culture from nasopharyngeal swab

differential.name: Tuberculosis
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough with sputum can mimic a prolonged bronchitis, particularly in higher-risk patients.
differential.trigger: Cough lasting more than 3 weeks with night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis or a compatible exposure history

history: Cough for weeks to months
Night sweats, fever and weight loss
Hemoptysis
Born in or travel to a high-prevalence country, incarceration, homelessness or HIV infection
exam: Upper-lobe crackles or amphoric breath sounds
labs: Positive interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test
Positive nucleic acid amplification test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
imaging: Upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation or hilar adenopathy on chest x-ray

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough can be caused by reflux, and patients may report chest burning that is attributed to bronchitis.

history: Heartburn, regurgitation or water brash
Cough worse after meals or when lying down
No preceding viral illness
Symptoms improve with acid suppression
imaging: Ambulatory pH monitoring shows reflux if performed

differential.name: Postnasal drip syndrome (upper airway cough syndrome)
differential.why_considered: A common cause of persistent cough that can follow or accompany a cold.

history: Constant need to clear the throat
Nasal congestion and discharge
Cough worse at night or on waking
No fever or chest pain
exam: Cobblestone appearance of the posterior pharynx
imaging: Sinus imaging shows mucosal thickening if sinusitis is present

severity.mild: Cough with clear or white sputum, no fever or low-grade fever, normal vital signs, no dyspnea at rest, able to carry out daily activities
severity.moderate: More frequent cough with colored sputum, low-grade fever, mild tachypnea, chest tightness and wheeze, some disruption of sleep and work
severity.severe: Persistent cough with significant chest discomfort, fever up to about 101.8°F, tachypnea, wheezing and reduced activity, but no hypoxemia or respiratory distress at rest
severity.critical: Not a feature of uncomplicated acute bronchitis; respiratory failure, marked hypoxemia or toxic appearance should prompt reassessment for pneumonia, sepsis or another diagnosis

red_flags.finding: Shortness of breath at rest or hypoxemia (SpO2 below 92%)
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pneumonia, pulmonary embolism or another serious cause rather than simple acute bronchitis

red_flags.finding: High fever above 101.8°F with shaking chills
red_flags.meaning: Points to pneumonia or another bacterial infection
Requires evaluation for tuberculosis, malignancy, bronchiectasis or pulmonary embolism
No longer acute bronchitis; evaluate for pertussis, asthma, reflux, postnasal drip or other chronic causes
Raises concern for tuberculosis or malignancy

red_flags.finding: Focal crackles, dullness to percussion or egophony
Toxic appearance or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Suggests sepsis or severe pneumonia; needs urgent evaluation

complications.name: Post-tussive vomiting and rib pain
clues: Chest wall soreness reproducible on palpation

complications.name: Rib fracture from severe coughing
clues: Focal chest wall pain worse with deep breath or movement

complications.name: Exacerbation of underlying asthma or COPD
Syncope with coughing
clues: Loss of consciousness immediately after a coughing paroxysm

special_populations.differences: Young children cannot describe sputum or chest tightness; they present with a lingering cough after a cold, sometimes with vomiting after coughing spells. Wheezing is more prominent and the cough may be mistaken for asthma or a foreign body.
Fever may be blunted or absent and the cough can be less forceful. Symptoms overlap more with pneumonia, heart failure and COPD, so the threshold for chest imaging is lower.
The same symptoms can progress to pneumonia or be caused by unusual organisms; fever and systemic symptoms may be more prominent and the course more prolonged.
Presentation is similar, but cough and shortness of breath are more alarming because of the risk to the fetus; treatment choices are limited and pertussis should be considered.

key_questions.question: How long have you had the cough, and how did it start?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset a few days after a cold; cough present for about 1–3 weeks, not more than 8 weeks

key_questions.question: Are you coughing anything up, and what does it look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Clear, white or colored sputum; purulent sputum alone does not mean bacterial infection

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, and how high did it get?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent or low-grade fever; high fever with shaking chills suggests pneumonia

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath at rest or with minimal activity?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; dyspnea at rest or hypoxemia points away from simple acute bronchitis

key_questions.question: Have you coughed up any blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; hemoptysis requires evaluation for tuberculosis, malignancy, bronchiectasis or pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Does the chest pain get worse when you take a deep breath or lie flat?
key_questions.looking_for: Chest soreness from coughing rather than pleuritic pain; pleuritic pain suggests pneumonia or pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Have you had a runny or stuffy nose, sore throat or hoarse voice?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent or current upper respiratory symptoms supporting a viral cause

key_questions.question: Have you been wheezing, or do you have a history of asthma or COPD?
key_questions.looking_for: Wheeze can occur with bronchitis; known asthma or COPD raises concern for an exacerbation instead

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, or are you around secondhand smoke, dust, fumes or vapors?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking or irritant exposure as a risk factor and a reason for a prolonged cough

key_questions.question: Have you had night sweats, weight loss or a cough lasting more than 3 weeks?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present raises concern for tuberculosis or malignancy

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you had a similar cough, or has anyone been diagnosed with whooping cough?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts; a contact with prolonged cough suggests pertussis

key_questions.question: Does the cough come in violent spells, and do you vomit or make a whooping sound afterward?
key_questions.looking_for: Paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting or whoop suggests pertussis

key_questions.question: Have you been hospitalized recently or taken antibiotics?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent healthcare exposure or antibiotics, which would broaden the differential

key_questions.question: Do you have heartburn or a cough that is worse after meals or when lying down?
key_questions.looking_for: Reflux symptoms that would suggest gastroesophageal reflux as the cause of cough

reasoning_points: A cough that began gradually after a cold and has lasted about 1–3 weeks, often productive of clear, white or colored sputum
Low-grade or no fever with sore throat, nasal congestion, hoarseness and fatigue supporting a viral upper respiratory illness
Chest soreness or tightness from coughing rather than pleuritic pain, and no dyspnea at rest
Lung exam with wheezing or rhonchi that clears with coughing, and no focal crackles, dullness to percussion or egophony
Normal or near-normal vital signs without hypoxemia, tachypnea or high fever
Chest x-ray not required when the presentation is typical; when obtained it is normal without consolidation
Pneumonia excluded by the absence of high fever, focal lung findings, hypoxemia and systemic toxicity
Pertussis considered and excluded when the cough is not paroxysmal and there is no post-tussive vomiting or whoop
Asthma or COPD exacerbation considered and excluded by the absence of a compatible chronic history
Antibiotics are not indicated for viral acute bronchitis; treatment is supportive

easy: Young or middle-aged adult with a cough for 1–2 weeks after a cold
Clear or white sputum, low-grade or no fever, normal vital signs
Diffuse wheeze or rhonchi that clears with coughing and no focal crackles
No dyspnea at rest and no hypoxemia
medium: Patient with purulent yellow-green sputum and mild fever, raising the question of antibiotics
Wheezing in a patient with no prior asthma history
Cough persisting 3–6 weeks after other cold symptoms have resolved
Older adult or smoker with overlapping COPD symptoms
hard: Older adult with blunted fever and a less forceful cough, where pneumonia must be excluded
Patient with underlying asthma or COPD where an exacerbation is the more likely diagnosis
Prolonged cough with post-tussive vomiting or whoop suggesting pertussis
Cough lasting more than 8 weeks, which is no longer acute bronchitis
Immunocompromised or pregnant patient with cough and dyspnea, where the threshold for imaging is lower
